newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Phnom Penh lawlessness takes toll on prostitution.
newsitem.headline: Phnom Penh lawlessness takes toll on prostitution.

text.p: Squalid in the best of times, prostitution in Phnom Penh is now unprofitable as well.

Customers who used to flock to brothels are staying home in droves, frightened by the political turmoil and general lawlessness in Cambodia's capital following a violent coup over the weekend of July 5-6.
"Before the fighting we used to get 10 customers a day but now we get only two," said Lang, 38, proprietress of a brothel at Svay Pak, a centre for prostitution north of the city.

"The fighting and looting really hurt our business. Even Cambodians are afraid to come here now, especially at night. They're afraid they may be robbed or beaten, even though it's safer here than it is in the centre of Phnom Penh."
When the occasional car, usually with dark, tinted windows, enters Svay Pak's main street, girls in bright dresses jump to the kerb, pouting and primping to advertise their services.
As the vehicle moves on the girls slouch back into their plastic chairs in the ground-floor, open-air 'reception areas' found in each concrete brothel.
Seconds later the young women are once again immersed in one of the televised soap operas they spend their days watching.
"I'm not making any money at all," complained 21-year old Nga, a plump Vietnamese girl in a shimmering pink dress and midnight makeup in mid-afternoon.
"It used to be we had a lot of business, especially in the evening, but now it's quiet all the time. I'm thinking about going back to Vietnam to become a cook."
Svay Pak caters to government officials and businessmen, both Cambodian and foreign, who can afford the girls' flat rate of five American dollars for a 'session'.
Some in that pool of potential customers have fled the country since the troubles and most others are cautious about driving 11 kilometres (seven miles) outside the city after dark.
As for Lang, the Vietnamese proprietress, who said she gets only two dollars out of every five her ten girls bring in, she wants to sell her business and go 'respectable'.
"I am making four dollars a day which is not enough to feed the girls and my husband and children," she explained.
"This is a hard life even when we have customers. Now it is too difficult. If someone would make me an offer I would sell. I would like to run a grocery in the market."
Svay Pak's corner kiosks, which carry a narrow, practical range of goods including women's underwear, cigarettes and condoms, are also suffering from a lack of business.
"Haven't sold anything all day except a black brassiere and three packets of 555's (cigarettes)," said a boy running one shop. "Business has never been this bad before."
Closer to town is Tuol Kork, where Phnom Penh's bargain basement brothels are found.

The flat rate in this district of wood shanties on stilts is just two dollars. Bored girls hang out under corrugated tin awnings festooned with tiny cardboard pennants advertising Tiger beer, Red Crown wine and Marlboro cigarettes.
Mud in the central lane is churned ankle deep in places by passing motorbikes and construction vehicles.
Girls here spend little effort trying to attract business, preferring to sit in clutches listening to pop music and combing one another's hair to fight the boredom.
Occasionally a motorbike pulls off the lane and roars right into the brothel, reinforcing the area's frontier atmosphere.
"Our business is OK during the day, but at night there is nothing," said another Vietnamese brothel owner with her feet and long skirt tucked up under her on a wooden bench.
"Tuol Kork is dead since the fighting. We need more customers, but they are afraid to come here."
Neth Sokun Thearith, manager of a public health clinic at Svay Pak, takes little comfort from the respite in business among the prostitutes his doctors treat.
"Once the political situation stabilises, business will return, I have no doubt," the manager said.
"About 30 percent of the 400 girls in Svay Pak are infected with some sexually transmitted disease. We treat them and educate them about condoms but the health problems remain."
